response.title: Acids and Bases — strength, pH and neutralisation
response.summary: This lesson sets up the three ideas the rest of acid-base chemistry rests on: what makes an acid strong as opposed to concentrated, how pH measures hydrogen ion concentration, and what actually happens when an acid meets a base. Several points in the original notes needed correcting, and each correction is marked where it appears.
objectives: Distinguish acid strength from acid concentration.
Calculate pH from hydrogen ion concentration, and back.
Predict the pH after a neutralisation from the strengths of the acid and base involved.
Carry out a mole calculation with units and significant figures.

blocks.originalText: A strong acid is one that is very concentrated.
blocks.text: A strong acid is one that ionises essentially completely in water. Concentration is a different axis entirely: it is how much acid there is per unit volume. A very dilute solution of hydrochloric acid is still a strong acid, and a concentrated solution of ethanoic acid is still a weak one.

blocks.definition: An acid that ionises essentially completely in aqueous solution, so nearly every molecule donates its proton.
The amount of solute per unit volume of solution, in mol dm⁻³. Nothing to do with strength.

blocks.wrong: Strong and concentrated mean the same thing.
blocks.right: Strength is about how completely the acid ionises; concentration is about how much of it is dissolved. The two vary independently, which is why dilute strong acids and concentrated weak acids both exist.

blocks.caption: The two axes, with an example in each corner.

blocks.useWhen: You have a hydrogen ion concentration and want a pH, or the reverse with the antilog.

blocks.text: The version in the notes defines pOH, not pH. The two are linked: pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C, so it is a useful relationship, but it is not what pH means.

blocks.originalText: Universal indicator gives an exact pH to 2 decimal places.
blocks.text: Universal indicator gives an approximate pH from a colour, usually to the nearest whole number. Two decimal places needs a calibrated pH meter, which is why one exists.
Litmus goes red in acid and blue in base.
Neutralisation is acid + base → salt + water, and it is exothermic.

blocks.originalText: This is always exothermic and always gives pH 7.
blocks.text: Neutralisation is exothermic, but it does not always land on pH 7. Only a strong acid with a strong base gives a neutral salt. A weak acid with a strong base gives a salt whose anion is itself basic, so the solution ends up above 7; a strong acid with a weak base ends up below 7.

blocks.originalText: that is the end point which is the same as the equivalence point
blocks.text: The titration description is right: acid in the burette, alkali in the flask, indicator, swirl to the colour change. One refinement — the end point is where the indicator changes and the equivalence point is where the moles actually balance. A well-chosen indicator makes them nearly the same, which is what choosing an indicator is for.

blocks.problem: What mass of sodium chloride is 0.25 mol?

steps.text: Find the molar mass. Sodium is 23.0 and chlorine is 35.5, not 12 — 12 is carbon.
Multiply the amount by the molar mass.
The data has three significant figures, so quote three.

blocks.commonMistake: Reading the wrong relative atomic mass off the periodic table. Check the symbol, not the position.

studentAttempt.issue: Chlorine was taken as 12 rather than 35.5, and the multiplication then used 23.4, which is neither value. The method — multiply moles by molar mass — was right.

blocks.originalText: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by lowering the activation energy and shifting the equilibrium to the right.
blocks.text: A catalyst lowers the activation energy, which is right, and it does so for the forward and reverse reactions equally. That means it reaches equilibrium faster but shifts nothing: the position of equilibrium is set by the thermodynamics, not by the path.

blocks.wrong: Adding a catalyst increases the yield of a reversible reaction.
blocks.right: It increases the rate at which the yield is reached. Only changing concentration, pressure or temperature moves the position of equilibrium.

corrections.original: A strong acid is one that is very concentrated.
corrections.corrected: A strong acid is one that ionises essentially completely; concentration is a separate idea about how much is dissolved.
corrections.why: Strength and concentration are independent, which is why a dilute strong acid and a concentrated weak acid are both ordinary things.
The version written is the definition of pOH. The two are related by pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C, but they are not the same quantity.

corrections.original: This is always exothermic and always gives pH 7.
corrections.corrected: Neutralisation is exothermic, but only a strong acid with a strong base gives pH 7.
corrections.why: The salt of a weak acid is itself basic, so the solution finishes above 7 — which is the whole reason titration curves have different shapes.
Chlorine is 35.5, not 12; 12 is carbon. The method was right, so only the numbers needed fixing.

corrections.original: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by lowering the activation energy and shifting the equilibrium to the right.
corrections.corrected: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both directions equally, so it reaches equilibrium faster without shifting it.
corrections.why: The first half was right. A catalyst changes the path, and the position of equilibrium does not depend on the path.

corrections.original: Universal indicator gives an exact pH to 2 decimal places.
corrections.corrected: Universal indicator gives an approximate pH from a colour, usually to the nearest whole number.
corrections.why: Two decimal places needs a calibrated pH meter — that is what one is for.

openQuestions.why: Your notes describe the method but not the shape of the curve, and the two are usually taught together.

flashcards.back: One that ionises essentially completely in water.

flashcards.front: Can an acid be strong and dilute?
flashcards.back: Yes. Strength is about ionisation, concentration is about amount per volume.
pH = −log₁₀[H₃O⁺], with the concentration in mol dm⁻³.
pOH. It relates to pH by pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C.
No — only strong acid with strong base. Weak acid with strong base finishes above 7.
The end point is where the indicator changes; the equivalence point is where the moles balance. A good indicator makes them nearly coincide.

flashcards.front: What does a catalyst do to equilibrium position?
flashcards.back: Nothing. It lowers the activation energy both ways, so equilibrium arrives sooner at the same place.
About one pH unit from a colour. Two decimal places needs a pH meter.

quiz.explanation: Strength is about the extent of ionisation. Concentration, pH and rate all depend on other things as well.

quiz.prompt: Write the definition of pH as an equation.
quiz.explanation: The hydroxide version defines pOH instead.

quiz.prompt: Ethanoic acid is titrated with sodium hydroxide. The pH at the equivalence point is:
quiz.explanation: The salt formed contains the ethanoate ion, which is a weak base, so the solution finishes basic.

quiz.prompt: What mass is 0.25 mol of sodium chloride?
quiz.explanation: M(NaCl) = 58.5 g mol⁻¹, and 0.25 × 58.5 = 14.625, which is 14.6 g to three significant figures.

quiz.prompt: A catalyst is added to a reversible reaction at equilibrium. What happens?
choices: Nothing shifts; equilibrium is reached faster
quiz.answer: Nothing shifts; equilibrium is reached faster
quiz.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both directions by the same amount.

quiz.prompt: Why can a concentrated solution still be a weak acid?
quiz.answer: Because only a small fraction of its molecules ionise, however many of them there are.
quiz.explanation: Concentration counts molecules present; strength counts how many of them donate a proton.
